qs.q: A 55-year-old man with heart failure has a right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis shows fluid protein of 2.1 g/dL, serum protein 7.0 g/dL, fluid LDH 88 U/L, and serum LDH 300 U/L. Most likely type of effusion?
qs.e: Using Light's criteria: (1) Fluid protein/serum protein ratio (2.1/7.0 = 0.3) is <0.5. (2) Fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio (88/300 = 0.29) is <0.6. (3) Fluid LDH (88 U/L) is <2/3 the upper limit of normal for serum LDH (typically ~200 U/L, so 2/3 of 300 is 200). All criteria point to a transudate, consistent with heart failure.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 48-year-old woman with breast cancer develops a right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields fluid protein of 5.2 g/dL, serum protein 6.8 g/dL, fluid LDH 420 U/L, and serum LDH 310 U/L. Cytology shows malignant cells. Most likely type of effusion?
qs.e: Using Light's criteria: (1) Fluid protein/serum protein ratio (5.2/6.8 = 0.76) is >0.5. (2) Fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio (420/310 = 1.35) is >0.6. (3) Fluid LDH (420 U/L) is >2/3 the upper limit of normal for serum LDH (2/3 of 310 is ~207). All criteria point to an exudate, which is expected with malignancy.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 35-year-old man undergoes thoracic duct injury during left-sided neck dissection surgery. Two days later he develops a left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields milky white fluid with triglycerides of 210 mg/dL. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: A chylothorax is caused by lymphatic fluid (chyle) leaking into the pleural space, often due to thoracic duct injury. It is characterized by milky white fluid with very high triglyceride levels (typically >110 mg/dL or 1.24 mmol/L) and a high lymphocyte count.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 51-year-old woman has 5 months of progressive lower leg swelling. CXR shows bilateral pleural effusions and prominent right heart border. AST, ALT, and LDH are elevated; CK is normal. Most likely underlying disease?
qs.e: Recurrent pulmonary emboli → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure → hepatic passive congestion → elevated transaminases and LDH but normal CK (no myocardial ischemia).

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman of childbearing age presents with progressive dyspnea, recurrent pneumothoraces, and chylous pleural effusions. HRCT shows diffuse thin-walled cysts throughout both lungs with no zonal predominance. Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Young woman + diffuse bilateral thin-walled cysts + recurrent pneumothoraces + chylous effusions = LAM. Caused by TSC2 mutations leading to smooth muscle proliferation around airways and lymphatics. Worsens with oestrogen.

qs.q: A pleural effusion with protein >30 g/L and neutrophilic infiltrate develops following right lower lobe pneumonia. This is best classified as
o: Exudate from microbial invasion — suppurative pleuritis progressing toward empyema
Hydrothorax from elevated hydrostatic pressure in congestive heart failure
Chylothorax from lymphatic obstruction by reactive hilar lymphadenopathy
Transudate from reduced oncotic pressure secondary to hypoalbuminaemia
qs.e: An exudate (protein >30 g/L with inflammatory cells) from pneumonia represents suppurative pleuritis from direct microbial extension — one of the four principal causes of pleural exudate formation.

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman has 3 years of myalgias, chest pain, arthralgias, a friction rub, bilateral pleural effusions, and mild normocytic anemia. Most appropriate initial screening test?
qs.e: Multisystem inflammation + pleural effusions + friction rub in a young woman = likely autoimmune disease. ANA is the best initial screening test, followed by more specific antibodies.

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman has myalgias, bilateral pleural effusions, ANA 1:1024, and BUN of 30. Renal biopsy shows granular immunofluorescence staining with anti-C1q antibody. This pattern is most typically produced by which mechanism?
qs.e: Granular immunofluorescence = immune complex (type III hypersensitivity) deposition. Complexes are trapped along glomerular basement membranes, as seen in SLE.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pleural effusion is excess fluid in the pleural space. It can be transudative or exudative, indicating underlying systemic disease or local inflammation, respectively. Diagnosis involves imaging and pleural fluid analysis, with management targeting the underlying cause.

sections.p: Pleural effusion is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, the area between the visceral and parietal pleura. Diagnosis is suspected with clinical signs and confirmed by imaging.
b: Fluid can be transudate (low protein, due to systemic factors like heart failure) or exudate (high protein, due to local inflammation or malignancy).

sections.p: Severity is often described by the amount of fluid and its impact on breathing. Large effusions causing respiratory distress are considered severe.
b: No formal staging system exists, but clinical assessment of dyspnea and radiographic extent is used.

sections.p: Causes vary widely, often categorized as transudative or exudative. In low-resource settings, consider infections like tuberculosis and complications of heart disease.
b: Transudates: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome.
Exudates: Pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion), tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, autoimmune diseases (e.g., SLE).
Other: Pancreatitis, Dressler's syndrome, trauma.

sections.p: Symptoms depend on the size and cause. Small effusions may be asymptomatic, while large ones cause shortness of breath, chest pain, and cough.
b: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, dry cough.
Physical exam may reveal decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and pleural rub.

t.b: Detects fluid and its approximate volume. Blunting of costophrenic angle suggests effusion. Lateral decubitus views can show mobile fluid.
More sensitive than CXR for small effusions, helps guide thoracentesis. Can differentiate loculated from free-flowing fluid.
Provides detailed anatomy, identifies underlying lung pathology, and helps characterize pleural masses.
Crucial for differentiating transudate from exudate and identifying the cause. Fluid is sent for cell count, protein, LDH, glucose, cytology, and microbiology.

sections.p: Urgent attention is needed for signs of respiratory failure or complications like empyema.
b: Respiratory distress, hemodynamic instability.
Empyema (pus in pleural space), tension pneumothorax (if drained too rapidly).
Malignant effusion, leading to progressive dyspnea and cachexia.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause and relieving symptoms. Therapeutic thoracentesis may be needed for large or symptomatic effusions.
b: Treat underlying cause (e.g., diuretics for heart failure, antibiotics for pneumonia, antitubercular therapy for TB).
Therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve dyspnea.
Chest tube drainage for complicated parapneumonic effusions or empyema.
Pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusions.

sections.p: Follow-up depends on the cause and resolution of the effusion. Prevention involves managing underlying conditions.
b: Monitor for recurrence and resolution of symptoms.
Address risk factors for common causes like heart failure and infections.

sections.p: Other conditions can mimic pleural effusion symptoms or imaging findings.
b: Pneumonia (consolidation can appear as opacity).
Atelectasis (lung collapse).
Pulmonary edema (fluid in lung tissue, not pleural space).
Ascites (fluid in the abdominal cavity).

sections.p: Certain findings can be misleading, requiring careful clinical correlation.
b: Normal chest X-ray does not exclude small effusions.
Transudative effusions can occur in malignancy if the tumor obstructs lymphatic or venous drainage.
Pleural fluid glucose can be low in conditions other than infection, such as rheumatoid arthritis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe shortness of breath
Rapid heart rate or low blood pressure
Fever with cough and shortness of breath

faq.q: What is the difference between transudative and exudative pleural effusion?
faq.a: Transudative effusions are caused by systemic factors like heart failure, leading to low protein fluid. Exudative effusions result from local inflammation or disease, with higher protein and LDH levels.
Yes, if the underlying cause is treated effectively. Many effusions resolve completely with appropriate management of conditions like pneumonia or heart failure.
It can be. Pleuritic chest pain, which worsens with breathing or coughing, is common, especially with inflammatory causes.
